items.title: Blackstone Targets $3B Fundraise For Real Estate Secondaries
items.description: Blackstone is raising cash to pick up stakes in real estate from antsy private-market investors. Bisnow/Sasha Jones Blackstone Strategic Partners, the firm’s secondary business, is expected to raise at least $3B as part of the latest fundraising effort, which will be used to target acquisitions of core real estate interests at discounts to net asset value, anonymous sources told Bloomberg . The capital will be primarily deployed into funds with data center, rental housing and industrial assets, the sources said, requesting not to be named because the fundraising drive isn’t public. Blackstone declined to comment to Bloomberg and didn’t respond to Bisnow ’s request for comment Wednesday morning. Strategic Partners' last fundraising round closed in November 2023 with $2.6B in commitments. The latest fundraising effort comes amid growing demand for real estate secondaries as a growing number of limited partners in real estate investments look to cash out early. Real estate secondaries had a record year in 2025 with $20.3B in total volume, with 72% of market volume coming from general partners, the fund managers that run the investments and typically decide to sell, according to a February report from Ares Management Corp. There’s a growing demand for cash now among both money managers and limited partners, the investors that provide capital but take a more passive role in operations, that is fueling Blackstone’s latest fundraising effort, executives who spoke with Bloomberg said. Blackstone itself has in recent months turned to the secondary market to help meet investor redemption requests. The investment giant in September reached out to potential buyers from Blackstone Property Partners to cut a deal that would let some existing investors liquidate. Blackstone Property Partners is a multifund vehicle with $58B in combined assets that invests institutional capital in long-term, income-producing assets, including data centers, industrial assets and office buildings. The secondaries market has expanded at a rapid clip since 2022, when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates and sapped velocity from capital markets. By 2025, general partner-led secondaries had become the fastest-growing segment of the market. UK-based Partners Group launched its own fundraising round for a secondaries program this year, announcing $650M in commitments in June for a fund targeting $1.5B in total. items.title: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS
items.description: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS Home prices hold steady as supply reaches a 14-year high HOUSTON -- (November 11, 2026) -- The Greater Houston housing market saw a change in pace in October, offering buyers more choices while sellers adjusted to a shift in activity. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Housing Market Update, single-family home sales were 14.9% below last year's level, with 6,348 homes sold. The average home price held steady in October at $421,100, while the median price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. The number of homes on the market remained near record levels, with 40,253 single-family homes for sale, up 6.8% from last October. "Consumers are paying close attention to the economy and their household budgets, so it is understandable that some buyers are taking more time before purchasing a home," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "We typically see activity ease as the year winds down, but buyers who are still looking may have more time to find a home that fits their needs and budget." Housing Market Overview Across all property types, 7,485 properties were sold in October, down 15.1% compared with a year earlier. Total dollar volume dipped 14.6% to $3.06 billion. The number of active listings across all property types increased 4.8% to 61,965 Despite October's decline, single-family home sales through the first 10 months of 2026 remained within 2% of last year's pace. Stronger sales during the spring and early summer helped offset the declines recorded in recent months. Single-Family Homes Update In October, 6,348 single-family homes sold across the Houston area, compared with 7,458 during the same time last year. That represents a decline of 14.9%. October's single-family home sales were the fewest for any October in the past 10 years. However, total sales over the prior 12 months reached 87,433, remaining above the 2019 level of 85,685, the last normal year before the pandemic. The average price was virtually unchanged at $421,100. The median price was $320,000, which is 3.0% below last year's level. It is the lowest median price for any October since 2021, with an October peak of $335,000 in 2024. The average mortgage rate in October was 7.33%, up 108 basis points from a year ago, but still below the 7.62% recorded in October 2023. Buyers of a median-priced home paid an estimated monthly mortgage payment (including principal and interest) of $1,760.28. That is $134.79 more than a year ago but less than the $1,845.03 paid in October 2023, when both rates and median home prices were higher. "Affordability remains a challenge for homebuyers, and the possibility of a quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve before the end of the year could add further pressure to the housing market," said HAR Chief Economist Ted C. Jones. Homes spent an average of 59 days on the market, unchanged from last October. Pending sales, which represent homes under contract but not yet sold, declined 17.6% to 6,445. The market had a 5.5-month supply of single-family homes, unchanged from September and its highest level since 2012. Nationwide, there was a 4.8 months' supply, according to the National Association of Realtors. Broken out by housing segments, single-family home sales performed as follows: $1 - $99,999: increased 2.1% (97 transactions) $100,000 - $149,999: decreased 1.0% (191 transactions) $150,000 - $249,999: decreased 9.4% (1,339 transactions) $250,000 - $499,999: decreased 16.8% (3,368 transactions) $500,000 - $999,999: decreased 16.9% (1,061 transactions) $1M and above: decreased 11.6% (291 transactions) HAR also reports on existing single-family home sales, which fell 10.2% in October. The average price declined slightly to $428,790, while the median price was down 4.5% to $315,000. HAR will publish its October 2026 Rental Market Update on Wednesday, November 18. For HAR's Monthly Activity Snapshot of the October 2026 trends, please CLICK HERE to access a downloadable PDF file. Townhome/Condominium Update The townhome and condominium market also recorded fewer sales in October. Sales declined 23.5% year over year, with 336 properties sold compared with 439 last October. The average sales price increased 5.8% to $263,413, while the median price declined 3.7% to $197,500. Active listings climbed 5.6% to 3,586 properties. The supply of townhomes and condominiums expanded from 8.2 months to 9.4 months, while days on market edged up to 65 days. Houston Real Estate Highlights in October Single-family home sales declined 14.9% year over year. Pending single-family sales declined 17.6% to 6,445. Active single-family listings increased 6.8% to 40,253. The average single-family home price was flat at $421,100. The median single-family home price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. Single-family homes took an average of 59 days to sell, unchanged from last year. The supply of single-family homes increased from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. Total property sales declined 15.1%, with 7,485 transactions. Total dollar volume declined 14.6% to $3.06 billion. items.title: J.P. Morgan Report, CoreWeave Earnings Provide Positive Signals For Data Center Construction In 2027
items.description: While the midterm election results sent a clear message that voters have concerns about the rapid data center build-out, it appears the industry's construction pipeline is still on track — at least for next year. Unsplash/İsmail Enes Ayhan New research from J.P. Morgan Asset Management and comments from CoreWeave leadership in the wake of its unexpectedly strong third-quarter earnings report point to a positive outlook for development in 2027, even if the sector is ultimately expected to lose steam in 2028. “We do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that’s occurred,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during the firm’s Tuesday afternoon earnings call. “We are very comfortable with our pipeline. ... We believe that what has occurred is a statement around how you build. We want to build responsibly.” “So we think that is an opportunity for us to continue to scale our business within the new political reality that exists,” he added. The AI firm's stock had plunged last week after anti-data center candidates swept the midterms, but it has been rallying since then, including a more than 26% jump since the earnings report was released Tuesday. CoreWeave reported $3.66B in quarterly revenue, up 168% year-over-year and beating industry estimates of $3.56B. It has also raised its full-year revenue guidance. The bullish outlook aligns with a projection from J.P. Morgan, which expects artificial intelligence -related capital expenditures to reach $1.5T in 2027 and level off in the following year due to political pushback, Semafor reported . J.P. Morgan researchers said in the report that the legislative pushback to data center construction has “more bark than bite.” Of the 16 statewide moratoriums that have been proposed, just one in New York has become law. The report also found that weeding out speculative projects could be good for the industry. It said of the 430 gigawatts worth of proposed data center projects, just 59% are in active development. “Projects already under construction are generally less vulnerable to new restrictions,” J.P. Morgan Global Market Strategist Stephanie Aliaga wrote. “Future developments face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing, with delays and higher costs potentially pressuring returns.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: CoreWeave , JPMorgan , Michael Intrator , Stephanie Aliaga

items.title: Household Debt Delinquencies Rise as Mortgage Performance Weakens
items.description: Household Debt Delinquencies Rise as Mortgage Performance Weakens November 11, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Household debt delinquency rates increased in the third quarter of 2026 as the share of delinquent balances and the transition to seriously delinquent debt increased. According to the latest Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, about 5.0% of outstanding household debt balances were in some stage of delinquency, an increase of 0.3 percentage points (pp) from the previous quarter. Total household debt balances that were seriously delinquent (at least 90 days delinquent) also edged up slightly from 3.3% in the second quarter to 3.4%. The deterioration occurred across several consumer loan categories. The serious delinquency rate for auto loans increased 0.2 pp to 5.7%, while mortgage delinquency rate increased 0.1 pp to 1.1%. In contrast, the serious delinquency rate for credit cards edged lower to 12.9%, although credit cards continued to have the highest rate among the major debt categories. Student loans displayed continued deterioration. The share of student loan balances that were seriously delinquent increased to 10.9%, from 10.6% in the second quarter. This marked a further increase in the proportion of student loan debt classified as seriously delinquent following the resumption of delinquency reporting. The flow of balances newly entering a serious delinquency stage showed a more mixed picture. Overall, 2.6% transitioned into serious delinquency during the third quarter, unchanged from the previous quarter. The share of student loan balances transitioning into serious delinquency declined to 7.7%, from 7.8% in the previous quarter. This followed a much sharper decline in the second quarter, when the transition rate dropped from 10.9% to 7.8%. Credit card transitions also improved slightly. The share of credit card balances newly entering serious delinquency decreased to 6.9%, from 7.0% in the second quarter, marking the third consecutive quarterly decline. Mortgage transitions, however, continued to move in the opposite direction. The share of mortgage balances newly entering serious delinquency increased to 1.6%, from 1.5% in the previous quarter. This category has been gradually trending upward in recent years, indicating continued deterioration in mortgage credit performance. Auto loan transitions remained relatively steady at 3.0%. items.title: Multifamily delinquencies up in October, driven by issues at San Francisco property
items.description: Multifamily delinquencies up in October, driven by issues at Bay Area property The CMBS delinquency rate is now at its highest level since December 2015, posting the largest jump of any property type over the past year, according to Trepp’s Stephen Buschbom. Published Nov. 10, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Dive Brief: The multifamily commercial mortgage-backed securities servicing rate rose 68 basis points month over month to 9.22% in October, according to Trepp Inc. Six months ago, it was 9.08%. A year ago, it was 8.32%. The multifamily CMBS delinquency rate rose 5 basis points month over month to 8.09% in September, partially driven by the $210 million mortgage against the 283-unit Cove at Tiburon apartment property in Tiburon, California, according to Trepp. Six months ago, the delinquency rate was 7.71%, and a year ago it was 7.12%. The loan at Cove at Tiburon matured in March 2025. A November 2025 modification extended its term through October 2026, when it went unpaid. Currently, a request to exercise a six-month extension, which could return the loan to performing status, is under review, according to Trepp. Dive Insight: The CMBS delinquency rate is now at its highest level since December 2015 and has posted the largest jump of any property type over the past year, according to Stephen Buschbom, head of applied research and analytics at Trepp. The servicing rate is at its highest level since December 2014. “There's also a lot of movement underneath that small net change,” Buschbom told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. Buschbom said about $398 million of conduit and single-borrower multifamily loans became newly delinquent in October, led by the Cove at Tiburon loan, while about $211 million cured. “Three of the new delinquencies were Houston loans written in 2025, loans that are barely a year old,” Buschbom said. In addition, Buschbom said Freddie Mac's K-Series multifamily delinquency rate rose to 0.96% in October, up from 0.8% in September and 0.55% in May. “That's still low, but the direction is clear, and October's increase came from borrowers missing payments, not from loans failing to refinance at maturity,” he said. The overall commercial real estate CMBS delinquency rate fell 15 bps MOM to 7.87% in October, while the CRE servicing rate rose 25 bps to 11.74% — the highest mark since December 2012. Office and retail delinquencies rose during the month, while lodging and industrial rates fell. Lodging, mixed-use and industrial helped drive the increase in servicing, while office and retail declined. At the end of the second quarter, CMBS and private securitizations were about 3% of outstanding multifamily mortgage debt , according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. items.title: High Housing Costs Keep Homeowners Locked-In
items.description: High Housing Costs Keep Homeowners Locked-In By Hannah Jones Nov 11, 2026 Key Takeaways: Today’s typical mortgage holder pays roughly $1,300 in principal and interest a month. To buy in today’s market, it would require roughly $1,100 more a month, or an 85.3% increase in mortgage payments. This translates to a 15.6 percentage point increase in the share of income the typical U.S. household spends on housing. The markets where mortgage holders face the steepest increase in mortgage payments include San Jose, Portland, ME, and Los Angeles. The least ‘locked-in’ markets, or markets where today’s mortgage payment requires the smallest increase to current mortgage holders, include Pittsburgh, Baltimore and Buffalo. At today’s home price, mortgage rates would need to be 6.0% or below for half of households to be able to afford a median-priced home. This would still mean a 61.7% increase in typical P&I payment. The Housing Market is Unlocking, but Very Slowly Record-low mortgage rates in 2020 and 2021, combined with surging homebuyer demand, produced a boom in both purchase and refinance activity. Roughly 27% of the most recent fixed-rate mortgages on record for U.S. single-family homes and condos were originated in just 2020 and 2021, and about two-thirds of them were refinances. Put differently, more than one in four homes with a mortgage on record carries a loan from 2020 or 2021 alone . Once mortgage rates began rising in 2022, both homebuying and refinancing collapsed. In the four and a half years between 2022 and the most recent data in July 2026, a period more than twice as long as the pandemic boom period, only about one in four mortgages on record (25.3%) was originated, underscoring how sharply activity slowed once rates climbed. In the 12 months ending July 2026, just 4.3 million mortgages were originated, only 6.6% of all mortgages on record. The latest data from the FHFA shows a similar pattern, as just 22.5% of outstanding mortgages carry a rate of 6% or higher, and more than 40% (42.8%) have a tenure of 5 to 7 years, which traces back to roughly mid-2019 through mid-2022. For those who purchased before mortgage rates shot sharply higher, the sentiment of “I couldn’t afford to buy my home today” continues to ring true in most cases, contributing to historically low mobility and some of the leanest for-sale inventory on record. Nationally, the estimated typical monthly mortgage payment is $1,300 year-to-date in 2026, and the typical mortgage rate on an outstanding loan was 4.0%. To purchase a median-priced home (as of Sept. 2026) at a rate of 7.32% (10/22 rate), assuming a 14.3% down payment, would mean a monthly principal and interest payment of nearly $2,500, or an 85.3% increase. In roughly one-third of the 100 largest metros, a move to a median-priced home would more than double their monthly P&I payment. Since our last report in December 2025, the benchmark rate has moved against would-be movers. Buying the median-priced home with a 14.3% down payment at today’s 7.32% rate costs about $2,470 a month in principal and interest, roughly $255 more than the same purchase at the 6.25% rate used in last year’s edition, which on its own widens the gap by about 19 points (66% to 85%). At the same time, the share of outstanding mortgages with a rate below 6% slipped from 79.8% to 77.5% over the past year, and the share below 3% edged down from 20.2% to 19.2%, a sign that unlocking is happening, but slowly. Low-priced, Accessible Markets See Smallest Lock-in Effect Affordable markets, mainly in the Midwest and the South, see the smallest lock-in effects, which has helped keep home sales activity comparatively resilient even as much of the country has experienced a more pronounced freeze in activity. The affordability of these markets enables mobility, which means the typical outstanding mortgage rate is higher, which helps reduce the payment jump associated with moving, which reinforces affordability. Roughly 75% of mortgages have a rate below 6% in the South and Midwest, compared to 78% nationally. Some of these affordable refuge markets have seen more activity in recent years as local home shoppers are able to move within-metro, and out-of-market shoppers look for shelter in these low-cost metros. Lower housing costs are only part of the story. Many of these metros also entered the current cycle with higher average outstanding mortgage rates due to some combination of a less intense pandemic sales boom, fewer refinances, partly due to smaller loan balances that reduced the incentive to refinance, and steadier sales activity in the high-rate environment of 2022 through the present. items.title: October 2026 Central Texas Housing Report
items.description: October 2026 Central Texas Housing Report 11/11/2026 Central Texas home sales decline in October as buyers navigate affordability challenges AUSTIN, Texas — According to the October 2026 Central Texas Housing Report released by Unlock MLS , closed sales across the Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos MSA declined 11.4% year over year to 2,114. items.title: Institutions Maintain Target Allocations to Real Estate
items.description: Institutions Maintain Target Allocations to Real Estate Institutional target allocations to real estate hold steady at 10.7% in 2026 following the survey’s first decline in 2025, according to the 14th annual Institutional Real Estate Allocations Monitor, published by Hodes Weill, a Chatham Financial Company, and Cornell University’s Baker Program in Real Estate. Institutions expect to increase target allocations by 10 basis points to 10.8% in 2027. After rising more than 20% between 2013 and 2022, target allocations have remained relatively flat since 2021. Approximately 54% of institutions report being under-allocated, up from 40% in 2025, representing the highest reported under-allocation since 2021. Meanwhile, the gap between target allocations and actual allocations widened by 30 bps year over year. The “Conviction Index” in this year’s survey, measuring institutions’ view of real estate as an investment opportunity from a risk-return standpoint from one (least favorable) to 10 (most favorable), declined to 6.0 from 6.4 in 2025, matching its five-year low. Douglas Weill, senior managing director at Hodes Weill, said, “Institutions have held their target allocations steady through a period that tested confidence, as renewed interest rate volatility and geopolitical uncertainty delayed the recovery many investors anticipated coming into the year. The widening gap between actual and target allocations reflects strong public equity performance and implies meaningful capacity for new investment. While institutions remain cautious, many are positioning to invest selectively at reset valuations, and as distributions recover, this allocation headroom could support a renewed pace of investment.” Pictured: Hodes Weill headquarters, 50 Hudson Yards in Manhattan. items.title: Housing demand shows signs of stabilizing. Does your market?
items.description: Lower mortgage rates are helping stabilize housing demand even as inventory has declined, according to Logan Mohtashami's latest Housing Market Tracker . But a national housing demand signal doesn't mean every local market is following. And even within the same metro area, buyer activity can tell very different stories. The Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area in Florida offers a useful example. New pending listings across the metro area increased 20.2% year over year in October, according to HousingWire Data . A closer look at individual cities, however, reveals that the improvement was far from uniform. One metro, different patterns of buyer activity In Ormond Beach, Fla., new pending listings increased 116.7% year over year in October, rising from 72 in 2025 to 156 in 2026. Nearby Port Orange recorded an 80% increase, while Daytona Beach saw a 63.2% gain. But Deltona, one of the cities that gives the metro area its name, experienced a 24.3% decline. New pending listings fell from 136 to 103. New Smyrna Beach also recorded a decline of 25.3%. Different patterns of buyer activity. This chart compares weekly new pending listings in Ormond Beach and Deltona over the past six months. While both cities experience fluctuations in weekly activity, their October year-over-year trends tell different stories. Adjust the date range or select YoY to explore how each city's activity compares with its historical performance. For housing professionals, the distinction matters. A regional market can be gaining momentum while individual communities within it are moving in the opposite direction. Seasonality doesn't look the same everywhere Fall typically brings a slowdown in housing activity, but the timing and magnitude can vary significantly by market. That's why a change in new pending listings needs seasonal context. Consider the average weekly new pending listings in three Volusia County cities between September and October 2026: Ormond Beach: Increased from 28 to 31.2 per week, up 11.4% . Port Orange: Increased from 16.3 to 19.8 per week, up 21.5% . Deltona: Declined from 26 to 20.6 per week, down 20.8% . Historical trends add another layer. Ormond Beach also experienced an increase in average weekly new pending listings between September and October in 2025, but the increase was smaller. Deltona experienced an increase during that period in 2025 before reversing direction this year. The lesson isn't that one city is stronger than another. It's that seasonal changes can play out differently even in neighboring communities. A decline in new pending listings may be consistent with a market's typical seasonal pattern. A smaller-than-usual decline could signal improving momentum. And an increase in activity deserves a closer look to determine whether it represents a sustained shift or a short-term fluctuation. What to watch in your own market The Florida example raises a useful question: Are changes in buyer activity consistent across the communities you serve, or is the broader market trend masking important differences? Four metrics can help you recognize changes, understand what they might signal and put that information to work. 1. New pending listings: Is buyer activity gaining momentum? What to watch: Compare new pending listings with the same period last year and track changes over several consecutive weeks. Look for activity that differs from the market's typical seasonal pattern. What it could mean: Sustained increases may indicate strengthening buyer activity, while declines can signal weakening demand. A smaller-than-usual seasonal decline may also be an early sign of stabilization. How to use it: Identify communities where buyer activity is changing. Agents can use that information to set expectations with buyers and sellers, while loan officers can help referral partners understand where transaction opportunities may be improving. 2. New listings: Is supply keeping pace with demand? What to watch: Compare the number of new listings entering the market with new pending listings. Is the gap between them widening or narrowing? What it could mean: When new pending activity increases relative to new listings, buyers may be absorbing a greater share of incoming supply. When new listings grow faster than new pending activity, more homes may be competing for buyers' attention. How to use it: Evaluate whether buyers are likely to encounter more competition or more choices. For agents, that can inform pricing and offer strategies. For lending teams, it can help identify markets where purchase activity may be gaining momentum relative to available opportunities. 3. Price reductions: Are seller expectations adjusting? What to watch: Track the share of active listings with price reductions and whether that share is rising or falling over several weeks. What it could mean: A rising share may suggest sellers are having difficulty attracting buyers at their initial asking prices. A declining share could indicate better alignment between pricing and buyer expectations, although changes in listing mix and seasonality can also influence the metric. How to use it: Bring evidence into pricing conversations rather than relying solely on recent comparable sales. Loan officers can use the same information to help referral partners understand negotiating conditions and where pricing expectations may be changing. 4. Days on market: Is the pace of the market changing? What to watch: Compare median days on market with recent weeks and the same period last year. Look for whether homes are spending more or less time on the market. What it could mean: Shorter marketing times alongside stronger new pending activity may reinforce evidence of improving demand. Longer marketing times, particularly when new pending activity is declining, may indicate that buyers are becoming more selective or that listings are taking longer to find the right price. items.title: BNPL for rent seeks a market
items.description: BNPL for rent seeks a market A new crop of fintechs is exploring growth opportunities in pay-later lending for monthly rent payments as inflation pinches consumers. Published Nov. 11, 2026 Justin Bachman Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Apartment buildings in Lower Manhattan, New York. Several fintech startups are drawing renters with pay-later services to cover monthly rent payments. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 13 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Pay-later loans are increasingly available for monthly housing payments as financial technology companies seek growth by responding to consumers’ affordability struggles. While the buy now, pay later market has traditionally focused on providing consumers with financing at retail merchants for discretionary items, a newer batch of companies sees profit potential in tailoring loans to rental payments and other monthly bills such as utilities, medical care and telephone service. A variety of players have moved into the pay-later rental arena in recent years, aiming to fill financial gaps between consumers’ monthly rents and their incomes, as the increases in the former outpace the latter. items.title: Rising appraisal defects signals likely stress for lenders
items.description: Rising appraisal defects signals likely stress for lenders By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 10, 2026, 5:52 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: The reason a recent drop in critical mortgage defects is actually cause for concern. Expert Quote: "Given this quarter's findings, however, appraisal will certainly be an area to watch next quarter" — Nick Volpe, Executive Vice President, Aces Quality Management Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Even as mortgage file defect rates improved on a quarter-to-quarter basis, the increase in appraisal-related problems is the canary in the coal mine for stress in a difficult housing market, Aces Quality Management warned. Processing Content The critical defect rate fell to 1.64% from 1.71% in the first quarter . But this is higher than the 1.51% for the second quarter last year , as the rate would eventually reach 1.79% in the following three months. While defects related to borrower income and employment returned to the most cited problem, increasing to 23.18% in the second quarter report, appraisal-related problems rose by 38.5% to a 4.64% share, the highest since the second quarter of 2025. Since Jan. 28, the mortgage industry has been in what was called the broad production period, as lenders could submit appraisals using either the UAD 2.6 or UAD 3.6 format to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. During this time, originators and appraisers were to use the opportunity to incorporate the new format into their workflows. Absent a waiver, mandatory use of UAD 3.6 started on Nov. 2. When asked if the switchover could be responsible for the rise in appraisal defects, at this point Aces has not seen any evidence in its data that the preparations for the change affected the category during the second quarter, Nick Volpe, executive vice president, said in response to an inquiry. "Approximately 60% of the exceptions were issues on the Form 1033 (post-closing appraisal review form)," Volpe explained. "These issues included: subject property eligibility, description of the subject property, Collateral Underwriter messaging, completion/inspection, and appraisal conditions that were unacceptable to Fannie Mae. None of those would lead us to believe that UAD 3.6 impacted the findings." Right now, it is hard for Volpe to comment on any future impact the switch could have on file quality. "Given this quarter's findings, however, appraisal will certainly be an area to watch next quarter, and it will be interesting to see if and how any of those manifest," he said. There isn't a defect category specifically for UAD 3.6, so any observations would be speculative." In the press release, Volpe pointed out that if appraisal defects hold in the 4% to 5% range in the third quarter data (since these are post-closing file reviews, the loans were originated in previous periods), "we'll want to dig into what's driving it." Refinances are another potential hot spot, precisely because the volume declined. The file which did come through and were reviewed "still carried a disproportionate share of defects," he said. "With rates higher in the third quarter, refinance volume may keep falling, and that's exactly when lenders need to stay disciplined on the files that do come through." Aces noted borrower and mortgage eligibility file issues rose a whopping 60.4% versus the first quarter to an 11.92% share overall, rising to third place. Meanwhile legal/regulatory/compliance defects fell by 17% to 21.52%. Aces categorizes mortgage file defects using the Fannie Mae taxonomy. Other categories with significant findings include assets, at 11.59%, an increase of 11.3% from the prior quarter. But Aces found fewer liability-related defects, at 9.72% and credit at 4.97%. items.title: Year-to-date home-sale growth narrows in Phoenix area with October home-sales dip
items.description: Year-to-date home-sale growth narrows in Phoenix area with October home-sales dip by Emily Marek November 11, 2026 Data from Phoenix REALTORS®' latest Local Market Update for Maricopa County. Home sales declined 18.2% year over year in Maricopa County in October as buyers closed on 3,214 properties, according to the latest data from Phoenix REALTORS® . That narrowed year-to-date sales growth to just 1.1% annually. A month prior, home sales were up 3.1% year to date. Meanwhile, pending sales also indicate slow sales in the coming weeks and months, decreasing 46.2% year over year to 2,147. Seller activity also stalled, with new listings dropping 9% year over year to 5,458. A total of 16,708 homes were on the market during the month, up 11.6% from October 2025. “Single-family home sales took a big hit for the month,” Phoenix REALTORS® President Sammy Glassman said in a press release. “Interest rates, economic concerns and the upcoming election all combined to make it a tough month.” The typical home sold in 71 days — five days faster than a year prior. Given the rate of sales, the county had a 4.3-month inventory, up 13.2% from 3.8 months in October 2025. The median sales price for October held steady just shy of $500,000. Meanwhile, the average increased 6.6% to $730,575. Year to date, the area’s affordability index has dropped from 76 to 70, meaning the median household income covers just 70% of the income needed for a median-priced home. “Buyers have more homes to choose from, and prices have remained relatively steady, but affordability continues to be a significant hurdle,” Glassman added. “Having more choices only helps if families can qualify for the mortgage.” Phoenix In Phoenix proper , closed home sales dropped 13.1% to 712 while pending sales plummeted 48.2% to 427. New listings also declined 2.7% year over year to 1,171. The city’s home prices increased: The median rose 2.6% to $481,998, while the average jumped 18.1% to $721,359. Given the rate of sales, Phoenix had a 4.2-month inventory, up 16.7% year over year. Scottsdale Market conditions were similar in Scottsdale as closed home sales fell 12.9% to 325 and pending sales dropped 43.5% to 208. New listings decreased 14.1% to 523. Amid that steep drop in new listings, the city’s inventory declined 4.5% year over year to 4.2 months. Meanwhile, Scottsdale’s median sales price rose 5.6% to $1.225 million and the average increased 6.9% to $1,618,450. items.title: Affinius Capital Provides $100.3M Construction Loan for Student Housing Project Near University of Pittsburgh
items.description: Affinius Capital Provides $100.3M Construction Loan for Student Housing Project Near University of Pittsburgh by Taylor Williams November 11, 2026 November 11, 2026 4 PITTSBURGH — Affinius Capital has provided a $100.3 million construction loan for Atmosphere Pittsburgh, a 672-bed student housing project that will be located near the University of Pittsburgh campus in the city’s Oakland neighborhood. The borrower is a joint venture between Starwood Capital Group and Trinitas Ventures. Atmosphere Pittsburgh will rise 10 stories and offer 326 fully furnished units, 34 of which will be designated as affordable housing. Shared amenities will include a rooftop fitness center and hot tub, game room, TV and computer lounges and private study spaces. Dwell Design Studio is the project architect. Completion is slated for summer 2028.
